row.note: The commentary makes truth something members pass to one another; Zechariah commands neighbors to speak truth to each other and judge for peace, turning haqq into communal practice.
The ayah's repeated reciprocal counsel is concrete here: Israel must reprove a neighbor openly rather than harbor hatred, making correction a duty owed to another.
The commentary stresses that each person gives and receives counsel; Proverbs explicitly pictures one person sharpening another, a close image of reciprocal moral strengthening.
The ayah's haqq is passed among a community; Paul tells each member to put away falsehood and speak truth with a neighbor, making truth an interpersonal obligation.

row.basis: stir one another to good works
row.note: The commentary says the righteous are defined by mutual exhortation, not only private belief; Hebrews tells believers to provoke one another to love and good works.
The commentary's repeated tawāṣaw makes support reciprocal; Hebrews names mutual encouragement as the community approaches the coming day.
The commentary warns that patience without haqq can harden into persistence in wrong; Hebrews says to exhort one another daily so no one is hardened by sin's deceit.
The commentary's two final verbs describe giving and receiving counsel; Paul likewise commands the community to encourage and build up one another.
The commentary makes sabr a shared practice; Paul asks the church to admonish the disorderly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone.
The commentary joins righteous action with counsel in haqq; John says love must be shown in deed and truth, joining ethical action to truthfulness.
The commentary's first three traits are belief, work, and patient mutual counsel; Paul praises a community's work of faith, labor of love, and steadfastness of hope in one compact formula.
The commentary makes belief and righteous deeds distinct but jointly identify the saved; James says faith without works is dead, insisting that belief must take visible form.
The commentary pairs belief with deeds; James reads Abraham's faith as active together with his works and brought to completion by them.
The commentary's exception includes both belief and righteous action; James explicitly says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone, a distinct reading of their relation.
The commentary describes the saved group by belief together with righteous deeds; Paul contrasts the one who does not work but trusts God, a different account of how faith is reckoned righteous.
The commentary's list includes righteous deeds among the marks of those rescued from loss; Ephesians locates salvation in grace received through faith, giving rescue a different source.
The commentary includes righteous deeds in its description of those who escape loss; Ephesians says salvation is not from works, directly contrasting the place deeds have in the two accounts.
The commentary includes righteous deeds in the saved group's defining pattern; Ephesians says people are created in Christ for good works prepared for them to walk in.
The commentary treats good action as work whose value is not lost; Hebrews says God remembers the readers' work and love shown in serving the saints.
The commentary places patience after truth and makes it communal; Hebrews urges imitation of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
The commentary links work, a due share, and the day when each meets what is owed; Paul says God repays each according to works.
The commentary's saved group persists in righteous work and patience; Paul describes those who seek glory through patient endurance in doing good.
The commentary makes patience the companion of truth and faithful action; Revelation identifies the saints by endurance, keeping God's commandments, and faith in Jesus.
The commentary links human work to the day of reckoning; the risen Jesus says his reward is with him to repay each according to their work.
The commentary defines the saved through righteous actions; in Matthew's judgment scene, feeding and welcoming the vulnerable count as service to the Son of Man.
The commentary sets righteous work against loss; Paul tells the community its labor in the Lord is not empty, directly answering the fear that work disappears.
The commentary joins work to the day each person receives what is due; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat and receive according to what they did.
The commentary makes sabr the strength to bear the cost of truth; Hebrews says believers need endurance so that after doing God's will they may receive the promise.
The commentary's sabr can mean standing as another's guarantor; Paul tells believers to carry one another's burdens, thereby fulfilling Christ's law.
The commentary's patience holds firm through hardship; Paul tells the community not to grow weary in doing good, since the harvest comes in its season.
The commentary joins inward restraint to good action; Jesus describes hearers who hold the word fast and bear fruit with endurance.
The commentary uses connected plants and patience through the season; James tells believers to wait like a farmer for the earth's precious fruit.
The commentary's sabr is remaining firm until the appointed time; James says to be patient and strengthen the heart because the Lord's coming is near.
The commentary joins faith, good work, and patience under threat; Peter tells sufferers to entrust themselves to the faithful Creator while continuing to do good.
The commentary calls patience a bitter medicine that can repair what it hurts; Hebrews says discipline is painful at first but later yields peaceful fruit to those trained by it.
The commentary's good action is a life that holds together rather than collapses; Jesus compares hearing and doing his words to building a house on rock.
The commentary pictures haqq as a straight thrust that reaches its mark; Hebrews describes God's word as a sword that pierces inward, making truth an active force.
The commentary distinguishes a fitting load from forcing a camel beyond its strength; Jesus says his yoke is easy and his burden light.
The commentary joins a load-bearing animal to the worker's due share; Paul cites the law not to muzzle the ox while it threshes grain.
The commentary links work with a rightful share; Paul says the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher in hope of sharing the harvest.
The commentary describes patient goodness turning hostility into intimacy; Paul applies Proverbs by telling believers to feed a hungry enemy.
The commentary presents patient good as the means by which enmity can become friendship; Paul concludes that evil is overcome by good.
The commentary's final example turns an enemy into a close friend through good conduct; Jesus commands love and prayer for persecutors.
The commentary joins work, connected growth, and due payment; Paul says planter and waterer are one and each receives wages according to labor.
The commentary's linked greenery pictures members who nourish one another; Paul calls the church God's field and its workers God's coworkers.
The commentary makes one person's due share a concern of the whole community; Acts says believers shared possessions so that no one among them was in need.
The commentary hears haqq as a debt owed by one person to another; the Lord's Prayer makes forgiveness of our debts reciprocal with forgiving our debtors.

row.basis: what is owed to a neighbor
row.note: The commentary says mutual counsel recalls what each owes the other; Paul says to pay what is owed and leave no debt outstanding except love for one another.
The commentary connects haqq with a debt and a worker's due share; James says unpaid wages cry out against landowners, exposing the injustice of withholding what is owed.
The commentary's guarantor image has one person holding another up; Paul says the body is arranged so its members have the same care for one another.
The commentary says when one member weakens another bears the load; Paul says if one member suffers all suffer, and if one is honored all rejoice.
The commentary's connected plants leave no gaps and feed each other; Paul pictures a body joined together as each part works and builds the whole in love.
The commentary brings work, payment, and the end of the day together; Deuteronomy requires paying a poor laborer before sunset because the wage is his livelihood.

row.basis: a burden too heavy for one person
row.note: The commentary says rightful loads fit capacity and patience can mean carrying another's share; Jethro warns Moses that judging alone will exhaust both him and the people because the task is too heavy.

row.basis: share the work among capable people
row.note: The commentary describes communal support as each holding what another cannot; Jethro tells Moses to appoint capable leaders so the burden is distributed.
The commentary names short measure and haqq as a due share; Proverbs condemns false balances and approves an honest weight.
The commentary says the Hāqqa brings each person face to face with their work and due; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, hidden or open, into judgment.
The commentary makes righteous action more than a label; Micah names the life God requires as doing justice, loving kindness, and walking humbly.
The commentary makes patience staying put in the hardest cold; Jacob recounts laboring for Laban through daytime heat and nighttime frost while sleep fled from him.
The commentary hears belief as entrusting oneself to safety; Jeremiah blesses the person whose trust is the Lord.
The commentary joins linked greenery to patient endurance; Jeremiah's trusting person is a tree by water that stays green in heat and keeps bearing fruit in drought.
The commentary's joined plants follow a rain-bearing cloud; Isaiah says rain and snow water the earth, making it sprout and provide seed and food.
The commentary treats advice as a word passed on for people to act upon; Isaiah says God's word goes out and accomplishes the purpose for which it was sent.

row.basis: the Lord is good to those who wait
row.note: The commentary interprets patience as remaining in place until the appointed time; Lamentations calls the Lord good to those who wait for him.
The commentary contrasts sabr with panicked outcry; Lamentations says it is good to wait quietly for the Lord's salvation.
The commentary describes sabr as staying firm through weariness; Isaiah says those who wait for the Lord renew their strength and do not grow faint.
The commentary hears belief as security and sabr as staying steady; Isaiah promises peace to the one whose mind remains steadfast because it trusts God.
The commentary's hard stone and mountain images make patience a form of firmness; Isaiah calls Israel to trust the Lord as an everlasting rock.
The commentary defines mutual counsel as a word passed among people; Deuteronomy commands parents to teach the words diligently and speak of them at home, on the road, lying down, and rising.

row.basis: assemble all to hear and learn
row.note: The commentary shifts from the singular human to a believing community; Moses commands the whole assembly, including children and resident aliens, to gather, hear, learn, and observe the teaching.
The commentary treats counsel as something that continues across a community; the next verse says children who have not known the law must hear it and learn reverence.
The commentary's good deeds are lasting and uncorrupted; Psalm 1 pictures the righteous as a tree bearing fruit in season whose action prospers.
The commentary sets those rescued from loss against the general human condition; Psalm 1 contrasts the fruitful righteous with wicked people like chaff that wind drives away.

row.basis: Noah righteous in a corrupt generation
row.note: The commentary's exception identifies those who escape the general human condition; Genesis calls Noah righteous and blameless among his contemporaries before the flood.

row.basis: Noah and those with him survive
row.note: The commentary opens an exception within universal loss; Genesis says all living things were blotted out except Noah and those with him in the ark.
The commentary's exception separates a community from general human loss; Peter recalls that only a few, eight persons, were saved through the floodwaters.
The commentary hears belief as reliance that gives security; Abraham trusts God's promise of descendants, and that trust is reckoned to him as righteousness.
The commentary's cloud image becomes rainfall; this verse says the sky grew dark with clouds and wind and a great rain followed.
The commentary's sabr image includes an animal held for death; the psalm's festival instruction binds the offering with cords to the altar's horns.
The commentary says believers need patience when threatened for their faith; one of the seven brothers chooses death rather than transgress ancestral law, a Jewish martyr scene of steadfastness.
The commentary hears iman as becoming secure; Isaiah's warning plays belief against being established, making trust a condition of standing firm.
The commentary describes sabr as waiting without loosening one's hold; Habakkuk says the vision has an appointed time and commands the reader to wait though it seems slow.
The commentary puts haqq before sabr as the ground for endurance; Habakkuk joins the righteous person's life to faithfulness while the vision is awaited.
The commentary says the repeated advice names truth so that harmful speech is not passed along; Zechariah forbids devising evil and false oaths after commanding truthful speech.
The commentary makes counsel and the other's due part of a shared life; Leviticus closes its instructions on honest dealing by commanding love of one's neighbor.
The commentary says one believer should remind another of what is owed; Proverbs says open rebuke is better than concealed love.
The commentary's counsel can be corrective as well as comforting; Proverbs calls a friend's wounds faithful, unlike an enemy's abundant kisses.
The commentary links work to a due wage and the danger of loss; Qohelet asks what a person gains from all the toil expended under the sun, making the outcome of labor a live question.
The commentary makes haqq something reliable that must be passed on; the psalm says the sum of God's word is truth and its righteous judgments endure.

row.basis: others hold up a weary leader
row.note: The commentary describes sabr as one person standing behind another when they weaken; Aaron and Hur support Moses' hands until sunset so Israel can continue the fight.
The commentary uses sabr as communal support; the Talmud rereads Moses' raised hands, saying Israel prevailed by looking upward and submitting their hearts to God, not by the hands themselves.
The commentary links work, time, and patience through hardship; Jacob's account of heat, frost, and sleepless service gives a lived scene of endurance within labor.
The commentary's haqq means what is right and binding; Moses asks what nation has statutes and judgments as righteous as Israel's, giving a concrete scriptural form of binding right.
The commentary opens against the human condition of loss; the psalm's speaker says that under the Lord's care he lacks nothing, a contrasting picture of provision.

The commentary distinguishes self-restraint in sabr from being held back by another; Sarai says the Lord has restrained her from bearing children, showing the same holding image with a different agent and object.
The commentary recalls a heap of goods taken without weighing; Job says the wicked may pile up silver and clothing, echoing the material heap image without making it patience.
The commentary presents counsel as a word that joins one generation to the next; Avot opens with Moses receiving and handing on Torah through a chain of teachers.
The commentary treats righteous actions as what keeps people from loss; Avot says the world stands on Torah, worship, and acts of lovingkindness.
The commentary's reciprocal verb makes each person both giver and receiver of counsel; Avot advises acquiring both a teacher and a companion.
The commentary insists that the saved are identified by work as well as belief; Avot says action, not study alone, is the essential thing.

row.basis: work that one must not abandon
row.note: The commentary describes patience as holding steady until work bears fruit; Avot says one need not finish the work but is not free to desist from it.

row.basis: deeds with this-world and future fruit
row.note: The commentary notes that this ayah names no wage after the opening faith-and-work formula; Peah says acts of lovingkindness yield fruit in this world while their principal remains for the world to come.
The commentary's plant image makes each cluster feed the next; Honi's old man plants a carob tree whose fruit he will not live to eat because others planted for him.
The commentary defines sabr as holding firm when hardship has no exit; Sirach tells the one serving God to accept what comes and be patient when humbled.
Onkelos renders Abraham's trust as belief in the Lord's Memra and reckons it as merit; this Jewish interpretation makes the commentary's trust in a promise explicitly mediated through God's word.
The commentary calls patience a bitter medicine that improves the person; Wisdom says the righteous were tested like gold in a furnace and found acceptable.
The commentary says people who speak truth may bear its cost; James points to the prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as examples of suffering and patience.
The commentary's sabr holds firm in pain and waits for the outcome; James calls Job's endurance blessed and points to the Lord's compassionate end.
The commentary pairs belief with work; Hebrews says Abraham obeyed and went out by faith, showing trust enacted rather than only asserted.
The commentary joins belief to deeds that define the believer; Hebrews says Abraham offered Isaac by faith when tested.
The commentary connects work to the day's wage; the vineyard owner pays the workers at evening, giving a narrative setting for labor, time, and compensation.
The commentary observes that this ayah names mutual counsel instead of a wage; Jesus says the Father will repay the person who gives alms in secret, an alternate framing of good action.
The commentary pictures sabr as staying under hardship and haqq as a load scaled to capacity; Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come for rest.
The commentary sets an unweighed heap beside reward without reckoning; Jesus describes a measure pressed down and overflowing, linking giving to the measure returned.

row.basis: generous wage and the worker's claim
row.note: The commentary understands haqq as a due share; the owner insists he wronged no worker while paying from generosity, complicating a simple equation of work and proportionate reward.
The commentary says deeds distinguish those who leave loss; Jesus contrasts the hearer who does not act with the house that collapses in a storm.
The commentary warns that sabr can become endurance in the wrong thing; Paul describes a hard, unrepentant heart storing up wrath for the day of judgment.
The commentary hears haqq as what is owed; Paul says a worker's wage is counted as a debt, not a gift, making the payment sense explicit.
The commentary's linked vegetation lets one growth meet another; Paul describes different workers planting and watering while God gives the growth.
The commentary hears mutual advice as speech that is joined and transmitted; Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he heard to faithful people able to teach others.
The commentary emphasizes repeated advice and the joining of day to night; the Didache tells a learner to remember the one who speaks God's word day and night.

row.basis: seek the words of the saints
row.note: The commentary pictures each person as both recipient and giver of counsel; the Didache urges believers to seek the faces of the saints daily and rest on their words.
The commentary's sabr includes a guarantor who stands with others in their affairs; Clement says the strong should care for the weak and the weak should respect the strong.
The commentary's plant clusters stay connected and productive; Jesus says a branch bears fruit only by remaining in the vine, making continued attachment the condition of fruitfulness.
The commentary says righteous actions define the saved community; Jesus says visible good works can lead others to glorify the Father.
The commentary describes haqq as a debt or rightful share; the owner answers a worker by pointing to the agreed wage, making the claim of what is owed explicit.
The commentary's âmanû means belief heard as trust; Hebrew he'emin describes Abraham trusting God's promise, a semantic match for the table's unverified sound correspondence.
The commentary links belief with becoming secure; Isaiah plays he'aminu against te'amenu, believe against being established, but the table marks the root match as unverified.
The commentary makes sabr support another until strength returns; the verse calls Moses' hands steady with emunah while Aaron and Hur hold them, a lexical and scene-level echo.
The commentary joins belief, haqq, and patient waiting; Habakkuk's righteous person lives by emunah, here faithfulness, while awaiting the vision.
The commentary treats haqq as reliable truth passed between people; the psalm calls God's word emet, truth, from the Hebrew root listed as a sound correspondence to Arabic amn.

row.basis: Aramaic אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary hears iman as trustworthiness as well as belief; Daniel's opponents find no fault because he is faithful, an Aramaic use of the table's corresponding root.
The commentary's haqq is right that is also binding; Deuteronomy's righteous statutes use the Hebrew root ḥqq, a possible sound correspondence whose legal sense is not identical to haqq.
The commentary frames humanity as being in loss; the psalm says the shepherded speaker will not lack, using the Hebrew root the table aligns with kh-s-r, though the Arabic root link is unverified.
The commentary explicitly recalls ṣabra as an unmeasured heap of goods; Job uses Hebrew ṣbr for piling silver, a specific heap image, not a claim that Hebrew ṣbr means patience.
The commentary calls ṣāliḥ action sound and fruitful; the righteous tree's deed prospers with Hebrew ṣlḥ, a possible root correspondence whose sense is success, not the Arabic adjective.
The commentary pairs sabr's self-restraint with ʿaṣr as holding back; Genesis uses Hebrew ʿṣr when Sarai says God restrained her from bearing, a possible sound link with a different agent.
The commentary's ʿamal is purposeful work; Qohelet's ʿamal is burdensome toil, a possible cognate that highlights a difference in the word's biblical use.
The commentary connects loss, a rightful share, and final reckoning; Daniel says Belshazzar was weighed in balances and found deficient, combining judgment with the market image.
The commentary identifies the saved by belief together with deeds; Jesus distinguishes saying “Lord” from doing the Father's will.
The commentary pairs belief with righteous action; James warns hearers to become doers of the word rather than deceive themselves by hearing alone.
The commentary makes sabr a shared practice; Paul names patience and bearing with one another in love as the conduct that preserves unity.
The commentary makes mutual advice a way of holding a community together; Jesus instructs a person to confront a sinning brother privately, and says listening can regain the brother.
The commentary joins correction with patience and self-restraint; Paul says to restore a person caught in transgression gently while watching oneself against temptation.
The commentary puts truth before sabr because speaking truth may carry a cost; Timothy is told to reprove, rebuke, and exhort with complete patience and teaching.
The commentary makes haqq the content of mutual counsel; Paul says love does not rejoice in wrongdoing but rejoices with truth.
The commentary describes sabr as holding fast for another; Paul says love bears, hopes, and endures all things.
The commentary's traits include work and patience; Revelation praises a church for its works, labor, and patient endurance while testing false claims.
The commentary pairs belief with righteous action; Peter urges believers to supplement faith with virtue and knowledge.
The commentary describes sabr as holding oneself steady; Peter's sequence joins self-control to steadfastness and steadfastness to godliness.
The commentary's virtues culminate in reciprocal counsel; Peter ends his sequence with brotherly affection and love.
The commentary calls patience a bitter medicine that forms the person; James says the testing of faith produces steadfastness.
The commentary treats sabr as remaining firm until its work is done; James says steadfastness should have its full effect, making the person complete.
The commentary says patient good can turn enmity into intimacy; Esau runs to embrace Jacob after their long estrangement and fear.
The commentary hears belief as security and counsel as something passed on; Jehoshaphat tells Judah to trust God and the prophets, with the promise that they will stand and prosper.

row.basis: a time to speak and be silent
row.note: The commentary joins truthful counsel to self-restraint; Qohelet's paired times for silence and speech give a concrete limit and occasion for words.
The commentary ties work to limited time and the day of reckoning; Qohelet urges wholehearted work now, saying there is no work or knowledge in Sheol.

row.basis: a soft answer turns away anger
row.note: The commentary imagines truthful counsel replacing dispute; Proverbs says a gentle answer turns away wrath, showing how speech can interrupt conflict.
The commentary says good conduct can turn an enemy into a friend; Proverbs instructs the reader to feed an enemy who is hungry.

The commentary reads kindness toward an enemy as reconciliation; Proverbs adds that feeding the enemy heaps coals on his head, a consequence often read as shame or repentance but whose force is debated.
The commentary links trust to safety on a journey; Moses recalls that God accompanied Israel through forty years of wilderness travel and they lacked nothing.
The commentary makes counsel reciprocal; Avot says that when two sit with words of Torah between them, the divine presence is among them.

row.basis: one good deed leads to another
row.note: The commentary pictures good action as work that keeps its value and continues; Avot says one commandment brings another and the reward of a commandment is another commandment.

The commentary replaces a wage formula with mutual responsibility; the Talmud lists acts of kindness and making peace between people among deeds whose fruit is enjoyed now while their principal remains for the world to come.
The commentary joins faith to patience under hardship; Sirach tells the one serving God to trust in the Lord, hope in him, and expect his help.
The commentary joins belief with haqq and sabr; Wisdom says those who trust God will understand truth and the faithful will abide with him in love.
The commentary treats patience as staying on a road through hardship; Hebrews urges believers to run the race set before them with endurance.
The commentary makes truthful counsel a communal duty carried with sabr; Peter says to answer anyone asking about hope with gentleness and respect, keeping a good conscience.

row.basis: bear with and forgive one another
row.note: The commentary's patience means holding together when people strain one another; Paul tells the community to bear with and forgive one another.
The commentary defines the exception by a completed pattern of belief, action, and patience; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved.
The commentary says truth may bring hardship that requires sabr; Paul praises the community's steadfastness and faith amid persecutions and afflictions.

row.basis: Aramaic חסר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary's khusr concerns loss and deficiency; Daniel's Aramaic says the king was weighed and found lacking, a close contextual echo whose root correspondence the table leaves unverified.
The commentary uses khusr for loss; Deuteronomy says Israel lacked nothing on its wilderness journey, a specific opposite use of the root candidate listed by the table.
The commentary hears iman as trust and security; this verse repeats the Hebrew root in “trust the Lord” and “be established,” a wordplay relevant to the ayah but not proof of cognacy.
The commentary labels righteous deeds with ṣ-l-ḥ; Jehoshaphat's line ends with the Hebrew verb for prospering, a possible sound correspondence whose biblical sense is success.
